A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Centaur and provide readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Relocated material can be matched reliably despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original data-reconstruction attacks, inference timing, communication measurements, and BERT/GPT-2 performance evaluations, including supplementary results.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds permutation-recovery experiments, feature-distribution analyses, and LLaMA-7B inference measurements.

M1.justification: The hybrid permutation/secret-sharing workflow, layer computations, and Algorithms 1–6 are retained. Appendix E applies the existing mechanism to LLaMA nonlinearities without introducing a different protocol. The client’s dealer responsibilities are newly explained rather than established as a procedural change.

E1.justification: The GLUE/WikiText tasks and CNN-DailyMail auxiliary data remain. v2 adds PIQA inputs to feature-distribution tests and permutation-aware attack scenarios with additional side information. LLaMA-7B extends model scale within the existing generation task.

E2.justification: The main MPCFormer/PUMA/SecFormer comparisons and SIP/EIA/BRE attacks remain. Appendix C.2 substantially expands the evaluated adversaries through RNN/linear feature classifiers and genetic-algorithm/gradient-based permutation recovery, extending comparisons beyond direct data reconstruction.

E3.justification: New evaluations vary the shuffled-feature fraction and introduce frequency, scoring-model, and ground-truth search controls. LLaMA-7B is tested with 4/8/16 input tokens and one output token at 20 Gbps/0.1 ms. The BASE-model 200 Mbps/40 ms timing cases disappear, although that setting remains in the LARGE-model figure.

E4.justification: v2 adds substantial analyses of partial-permutation sensitivity, feature-distribution similarity, classifier-based identification, and heuristic permutation cracking (Appendix C, Figure 7, Tables 4–5). The earlier direct reconstruction attacks, examples, and most efficiency breakdowns are retained or relocated.

E5.justification: Appendix C.1 newly reports fitting and smoothing the feature-shuffling response curve in Figure 7, adding a statistical estimation procedure. Existing three-seed attack averages, plus/minus reporting, and ten-run timing averages remain; the PDFs do not establish increased repetition counts.

E6.justification: The three matched attack/performance tables and LARGE-model timing and communication results are numerically unchanged. v2 adds sensitivity, distribution, cracking, and LLaMA results, including 2.76/3.02/6.81-second inference times in Table 6, while removing BASE-model WAN timing entries. Section 3 replaces the PUMA example (1066 seconds, 94 GB) with CrypTen (881 seconds, 66 GB), which is not a same-method improvement.

T1.justification: Theorem 1, its proof, and the distance-correlation inequality move substantially unchanged into Appendix B. v2 adds permutation-equivariance derivations for RMSNorm and SwiGLU in Appendix E and makes the excluded party collusions explicit in Section 4.2.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain hybrid privacy protection, accurate inference without model modification or retraining, and a claimed 5.0–30.4-fold speedup. Rewording and additional supporting experiments do not materially redefine these main claims.

C2.justification: New Discussion and Limitations sections explicitly acknowledge the lack of direct theoretical security and the absence of quantization/KV-cache integration. Appendix C substantially expands explanations involving inverse-mapping disruption, similar feature distributions, and contextual noise. These qualifications coexist with stronger retained theoretical assertions in Appendix B.

D1.justification: v2 adds permutation-cracking hardware, heuristic construction, stopping information, and details of the client’s dealer role. Existing attack and fine-tuning hyperparameters are retained. However, the explicit 16-bit fixed-point precision, task-performance metric descriptions, model-architecture summaries, and CrypTen repository link are removed.

R1.justification: The general neural-network privacy survey and its associated references are removed, while Transformer comparisons are integrated into the motivation. New references support three-party security, simulation, permutation search, and Nimbus. Appendix C also introduces a priority claim for thoroughly analyzing permutation-based Transformer security, substantially refocusing the positioning.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, preliminaries, and motivation undergo extensive rewriting and compression. Security and communication analyses move into appendices, the attack appendix is reorganized, and Discussion, Limitations, and Acknowledgements sections are added.

P2.justification: The overview is redrawn, the standalone Transformer diagram and motivation chart are removed, and the protocol-cost table disappears. v2 adds a sensitivity figure and three tables, removes two BASE-model timing panels, relocates existing displays, and reformats the appendices from one column to two.

improvement.justification: Permutation-aware attacks, LLaMA-7B measurements, and explicit security limitations improve the paper’s empirical support and transparency. These gains outweigh reduced reproducibility documentation, but new attack procedures remain incompletely specified and reporting inconsistencies persist. For example, v2 Section 5.2 claims 100% GPT-2 O1 recovery although its unchanged table reports 96.70%; Appendix B’s strong theoretical assertions also remain insufficiently reconciled with the new limitations.
